summary: An April 1st joke RFC. It proposes a supposed extra mechanism to ease the move from IPv4 to IPv6 while improving security and privacy. It is humor and not a real specification.

eli5.summary: A silly made-up plan for helping the old street-address system turn into the new one, written as a joke.

questions: what is the evil bit in ipv4
subtitle: An April 1st joke about security flags for both IPv4 and IPv6

tldr.problem: IPv4 has a security flag (RFC 3514, the 'evil bit') but IPv6 does not have an equivalent, creating an asymmetry between the two protocols.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC jokingly proposes that all IPv4 packets set the evil bit to 1, and defines an IPv6 security flag as the parity of the source address (odd number of 1 bits = True). An advanced option (UFO) adds a hop-by-hop flag field for more control.
tldr.outcome: This is an April 1st humor document and not a real specification. It plays on legal language about employment discrimination while explaining technical IPv6 concepts straight-faced.

today: RFC 8136 is clearly an April 1st humor document. It should not be implemented. It was published to entertain the networking community while playing with IPv6 concepts. The document is informational and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Joke Setup
sections.content:
This is an April 1st humor RFC, not a real specification. It humorously proposes solving an IPv6 security feature gap by requiring all IPv4 packets to set the evil bit (from RFC 3514) to 1, then defining an equivalent mechanism for IPv6.

The document uses employment law language to discuss packet discrimination, calling issues like TTL-based dropping 'age-based termination' and IP-version filtering 'discrimination.' Despite the humorous framing, the technical details are accurate to RFC specifications.
sections.eli5: The authors joke that networks discriminate against packets in unfair ways, like employers might discriminate against job applicants. The funny part is using employment law to talk about computers.

sections.title: The Proposals (Not to be Implemented)
sections.content:
The RFC proposes two approaches. The first defines the IPv6 security flag as the parity of the source address: if the source IPv6 address contains an odd number of 1 bits, the flag is True; otherwise False. Hosts can control this flag by choosing the Interface Identifier when they autoconfigure their address.

The advanced solution introduces a hop-by-hop User Security Flag Option (UFO) with a UserSecFlag field. Bit 0 carries the main security flag, and bit 1 optionally encodes a privacy flag. When the privacy flag is set, the RFC jokes that firewalls and governments 'MUST respect' the privacy request—a pun on the idea that nothing can guarantee actual privacy.
sections.eli5: One funny idea uses the address itself to store the flag. The other creates a new message option with a silly name (UFO).

sections.title: The Outcome
sections.content:
With all IPv4 packets marked as evil and the IPv6 flag defined by address parity, exactly half of the IPv6 address space would indicate the security flag is set, leading to the humorous conclusion that 'the IPv6 Internet is only half evil.' The RFC notes that implementing this would likely cause routers to treat all IPv4 traffic as a distributed denial-of-service attack.

The privacy flag extension is particularly absurd: simply adding a flag and requesting respect is proposed as being more computationally efficient than real encryption like IPsec or TLS.
sections.eli5: If you do all this, the jokes say half the internet is evil and privacy is solved by asking nicely.
